title: Fear none, frighten none
hookLine: bhai kaahoo kau det neh neh bhai maanat aan: frighten no one and fear no one; that one is wise (Salok M9, ang 1427)
tomorrow: Like a dream and a show

cards: Think of two kinds of people who make a room go tense. One is the bully: loud, threatening, used to getting their way by making others afraid.
The other is so afraid themselves that they'll agree to anything, betray anyone, to stay safe. They look like opposites. But they're often the same person on different days.
Fear going out and fear coming in are two ends of one rope. Guru Tegh Bahadur's sixteenth salok cuts that rope at both ends, in a single line.

teach.b: The salok says bhai kaahoo kau det neh, neh bhai maanat aan. In paraphrase: the one who gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one else: says Nanak, listen, O mind, call that one wise. Bhai is fear.
Det is to give. Maanat is to accept, to take on. The wise one, giaanee, is defined by both at once.
Sikhs hear this beside two words from the Mool Mantar: nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without enmity. Those describe God. This salok describes a person who has started to resemble them.
And Sikhs think of the man who wrote it.

Sikh tradition remembers that in 1675, a group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus, came to him at Anandpur. They said Mughal officials were forcing them to give up their faith. He listened, and set out for Delhi himself.
He raised no army. He threatened no one. On the way he was arrested and taken to Delhi.
When he was ordered to give up his own faith or die, he refused. He was executed in Delhi, at the place where Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands today.
Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, and remember that he gave his life for the freedom of people whose faith was not his own.
He didn't frighten his enemies, and he didn't let them frighten him. That's a very hard kind of courage, gentle and brave in the same moment, and the salok makes it sound almost simple.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year, especially at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, and often recite his salok on giving and taking no fear as the heart of his example.

o: giving no fear, and taking none on
staying silent so no one gets upset

s: the salok praises the one who makes enemies afraid
it calls wise the one who gives fear to no one, and takes it from no one.
Sikh tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur went to Delhi for people of another faith
Kashmiri Pandits asked for help; he gave his life for their freedom to practice.
Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi stands where he was executed
Sikhs remember him there each year.

games.q: it's 1675. Kashmiri Pandits come to Anandpur saying they're being forced to give up their faith. you're the Guru. what do you do?
o: raise an army and march on Delhi.
go to Delhi yourself, unarmed, and refuse to give up your own faith.
advise them to give in quietly.
games.why: Sikh tradition remembers that he set out for Delhi himself, was arrested on the way, threatened no one, refused to give up his faith, and was executed. frighten none, fear none.

practice: Think of one situation coming up where fear might show up on either end, where you might lean on someone too hard or give in when you shouldn't: a meeting, a family conversation, a moment of standing up for someone.
Picture yourself in it, speaking calmly and clearly, neither pushing nor shrinking, and feel your feet on the floor. If you pray, you can ask Waheguru for that steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Fear none. The sixteenth salok calls wise the one who frightens no one and accepts fear from no one, and Sikhs see it lived in Guru Tegh Bahadur's walk to Delhi.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhai, fear. The salok says: give bhai to no one, take bhai from no one.

carryVoice: Your line: frighten none, fear none. Neither pushing nor shrinking: the rope cut at both ends. Rest well tonight.
